title: Logistic Regression I - The Perceptron Trick
abstract:
The first step towards logistic regression, and a genuine algorithm in its own
right. The perceptron trick starts from the general equation of a line,
$Ax+By+C=0$, and adjusts $A$, $B$ and $C$ again and again until the line separates
the two classes correctly. This document covers why the general form replaces
$y=mx+c$, the geometry of the update rule and why it rotates the boundary towards
each mistake, the convergence theorem and its failure on non-separable data, and
— most importantly — the two defects that force the move to the sigmoid in
Topic 45.

blocks.t: The Setup
From the notes

items: Data should be linearly separable.

We use the general equation of a line here:
 $y=mx+b \;\longrightarrow\; Ax+By+C=0$.
Goal is to find $A$, $B$, $C$.

Perceptron trick: $A$, $B$ decide the direction of the
 line; $C$ decides where the line sits.

Adjust $A$, $B$, $C$ again and again till the line separates the
 data correctly, by comparing with a random point in each epoch.

blocks.cap:
Left: linearly separable data, and several lines that would work.
 Middle: why the general form is used. Right: the vector $(A,B)$ is normal
 (perpendicular) to the line, and the sign of $Ax+By+C$ tells you which
 side a point falls on.

blocks.t: Why $Ax+By+C=0$ and not $y=mx+c$
Three reasons the general form is needed

items:
$y=mx+c$ cannot represent a vertical line. A vertical boundary
 needs $m=\infty$. $Ax+By+C=0$ handles it with $B=0$.

It generalises to any number of features. In $n$ dimensions,
 $w_1x_1+\cdots+w_nx_n+b=0$ is a hyperplane. The slope–intercept form has
 no such extension.

The sign is the classifier. $Ax+By+C$ is positive on one side and
 negative on the other, so a single expression gives both the boundary and
 the decision rule.

blocks.t: The geometry
Write $w=(A,B)$ and $b=C$, so the line is $w^{\!\top}x+b=0$.

items:
$w$ is normal to the line: for any two points $x_1,x_2$ on it,
 $w^{\!\top}(x_1-x_2)=0$.

The signed distance from a point to the line is
 $\dfrac{w^{\!\top}x+b}{\|w\|}$.
The classification rule is $\hat y=\operatorname{sign}(w^{\!\top}x+b)$.

blocks.t:
So $w$ sets the orientation of the boundary and $b$ its offset
from the origin — exactly the notes' "$A$, $B$ decide the direction; $C$
decides where the line sits".
The Perceptron Trick
The algorithm
Label the classes $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$. Then:

items: Start with random $w$ and $b$.
Pick a training point $(x_i,y_i)$.
Predict $\hat y_i=\operatorname{sign}(w^{\!\top}x_i+b)$.

If it is correct, do nothing. If it is wrong, update:
 $$\boxed{\;w \leftarrow w+\eta\,y_i\,x_i, \qquad b \leftarrow b+\eta\,y_i\;}$$
Repeat for many epochs until no point is misclassified.

blocks.cap:
The boundary being adjusted. It starts random, swings sharply after the
 first few corrections, and settles once every point is on the correct side.

blocks.t: Why the update moves in the right direction

Suppose $x_i$ has true label $y_i=+1$ but is misclassified, so
$w^{\!\top}x_i+b<0$. After the update,

The added term is strictly positive, so the score for that point always
moves in the correct direction. The same argument with signs reversed covers
$y_i=-1$. Each update is guaranteed to improve the prediction for the
point that triggered it — though possibly at the expense of others, which is
why several passes are needed.

Geometrically, adding $\eta y_i x_i$ to $w$ rotates the normal vector towards
(for $y_i=+1$) or away from (for $y_i=-1$) the offending point, tilting the
boundary to put it on the right side.

blocks.cap:
Left: vector addition. The update adds a scaled copy of the misclassified
 point to the weight vector, rotating the boundary. Right: the step activation
 used by the perceptron, next to the sigmoid that replaces it in Topic 45.

blocks.t: The bias trick

Appending a constant $1$ to every input vector and absorbing $b$ into $w$ turns
the two update rules into one: $\tilde x=(x,1)$, $\tilde w=(w,b)$, and the update
is simply $\tilde w \leftarrow \tilde w+\eta y_i\tilde x_i$. This is the same
device as the leading column of ones in Topic 36.
Convergence — and Its Limit
The Perceptron Convergence Theorem (Novikoff, 1962)

If the data is linearly separable with margin $\gamma>0$ — that is, there exists
a unit vector $w^*$ with $y_i(w^{*\top}x_i)\ge\gamma$ for all $i$ — and
$\|x_i\|\le R$, then the perceptron makes at most
\left(\frac{R}{\gamma}\right)^{2}

mistakes before converging, regardless of the order of the data or the
learning rate.

Two things are notable. The bound does not involve $n$ or the number of
dimensions — only the geometry. And it says nothing when $\gamma=0$: on
non-separable data the algorithm never terminates, cycling forever.
The notes' condition is a hard requirement

"Data should be linearly separable" is not a suggestion. On overlapping
data — which is nearly all real data — the perceptron never stops and the
boundary keeps oscillating. There is no "best line" in the algorithm's own
terms, because its only objective is "zero mistakes".

The standard patch is the pocket algorithm: keep a copy of the best weights
seen so far. But that is a fix bolted on from outside, not a principled objective.
Two Defects That Force the Next Step
Defect 1 — any separating line will do

When the data is separable, there are infinitely many valid lines and the
perceptron returns whichever one it happened to stop at. A line that passes a
hair's breadth from the nearest point is accepted just as readily as one down the
middle — yet the first will generalise far worse.
Two different repairs exist, and they define two later topics:

items:
SVM (Topics 72–74) chooses the line with the maximum
 margin.

Logistic regression (Topics 45–46) chooses the line that
 maximises the likelihood of the observed labels.

blocks.t: Defect 2 — the output is hard, and the gradient is zero

The notes state it directly: the perceptron had a hard output of $0$ or
$1$. Two consequences:

items:
No confidence. A point sitting on the boundary and one far inside
 the region both get the same answer. You cannot rank customers by risk, and
 you cannot move the decision threshold (Topics 09, 53).

No gradient. The step function is flat everywhere and undefined at
 zero, so its derivative is $0$ almost everywhere. Gradient descent
 cannot be used at all — there is no slope to descend.

blocks.t:
This is exactly why the next topic replaces the step function with the sigmoid:
it is smooth, differentiable, and outputs a probability.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Perceptron, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE PERCEPTRON TRICK, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
A = rng.multivariate_normal([2.2, 2.2], [[.8, .2], [.2, .8]], 60)
B = rng.multivariate_normal([6.2, 6.0], [[.8, -.2], [-.2, .8]], 60)
X = np.vstack([A, B])
y = np.r_[-np.ones(60), np.ones(60)]          # labels are -1 and +1, NOT 0/1

def perceptron(X, y, lr=0.1, epochs=100, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = r.normal(0, 1, X.shape[1])            # A and B  (the DIRECTION)
    b = r.normal()                            # C        (WHERE the line sits)
    mistakes_per_epoch = []

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        mistakes = 0
        for i in r.permutation(len(X)):       # "comparing with a random point"
            if y[i] * (w @ X[i] + b) <= 0:    # misclassified
                w += lr * y[i] * X[i]         # w <- w + eta*y*x
                b += lr * y[i]                # b <- b + eta*y
                mistakes += 1
        mistakes_per_epoch.append(mistakes)
        if mistakes == 0:                     # separated -> stop
            return w, b, epoch + 1, mistakes_per_epoch
    return w, b, epochs, mistakes_per_epoch

w, b, epochs_used, hist = perceptron(X, y)
print(f"converged after {epochs_used} epochs")
print(f"A = {w[0]:.4f}   B = {w[1]:.4f}   C = {b:.4f}")
print(f"accuracy: {np.mean(np.sign(X @ w + b) == y):.4f}")
print("mistakes per epoch:", hist[:8])

# =====================================================================
# 2. EACH UPDATE PROVABLY IMPROVES THE OFFENDING POINT
# =====================================================================
w0, b0, lr = np.array([0.5, -1.2]), 0.3, 0.1
i = 0                                         # a point with y = -1
before = w0 @ X[i] + b0
w1 = w0 + lr * y[i] * X[i]
b1 = b0 + lr * y[i]
after = w1 @ X[i] + b1
print(f"\npoint {i}: y={y[i]:+.0f}  score before {before:+.4f}  after {after:+.4f}")
print(f"change = {after-before:+.4f}, predicted "
      f"{lr*y[i]*(X[i]@X[i] + 1):+.4f}   <- eta*y*(||x||^2 + 1)")
# The score always moves in the direction of the correct label.

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE BIAS TRICK -- one update rule instead of two
# =====================================================================
Xa = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(X))]                # append a constant 1
def perceptron_bias_trick(Xa, y, lr=0.1, epochs=100, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = r.normal(0, 1, Xa.shape[1])           # w now CONTAINS the bias
    for _ in range(epochs):
        wrong = 0
        for i in r.permutation(len(Xa)):
            if y[i] * (w @ Xa[i]) <= 0:
                w += lr * y[i] * Xa[i]        # ONE rule
                wrong += 1
        if wrong == 0: break
    return w
wa = perceptron_bias_trick(Xa, y)
print(f"\nbias trick: A={wa[0]:.4f} B={wa[1]:.4f} C={wa[2]:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. DEFECT 1 -- IT RETURNS AN ARBITRARY SEPARATING LINE
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'seed':>5s} {'A':>9s} {'B':>9s} {'C':>9s} {'min margin':>12s}")
for s in range(5):
    ws, bs, _, _ = perceptron(X, y, seed=s)
    margin = np.min(y * (X @ ws + bs)) / np.linalg.norm(ws)
    print(f"{s:5d} {ws[0]:9.3f} {ws[1]:9.3f} {bs:9.3f} {margin:12.4f}")
# Every run finds a DIFFERENT line, all with 100% training accuracy,
# and some pass much closer to the data than others.

# Compare with the maximum-margin solution an SVM finds (Topic 72):
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
svm = LinearSVC(C=1000, max_iter=20000).fit(X, y)
svm_margin = np.min(y * (X @ svm.coef_[0] + svm.intercept_[0])) / np.linalg.norm(svm.coef_[0])
print(f"SVM max-margin solution: margin {svm_margin:.4f}  <- the LARGEST possible")

# =====================================================================
# 5. IT NEVER CONVERGES ON NON-SEPARABLE DATA
# =====================================================================
Xo, yo = make_blobs(n_samples=200, centers=[[2, 2], [3.4, 3.4]],
                    cluster_std=1.3, random_state=0)
yo = np.where(yo == 0, -1, 1)                 # deliberately OVERLAPPING

w2, b2, ep, hist2 = perceptron(Xo, yo, epochs=300)
print(f"\noverlapping data: ran {ep} epochs (limit 300)")
print(f"mistakes in the last 8 epochs: {hist2[-8:]}")
print(f"final accuracy: {np.mean(np.sign(Xo @ w2 + b2) == yo):.4f}")
# It NEVER reaches zero mistakes -- the boundary oscillates forever.

# The POCKET algorithm: remember the best weights seen so far
def pocket(X, y, lr=0.1, epochs=300, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w, b = r.normal(0, 1, X.shape[1]), r.normal()
    best_w, best_b, best_acc = w.copy(), b, 0.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for i in r.permutation(len(X)):
            if y[i] * (w @ X[i] + b) <= 0:
                w += lr * y[i] * X[i]; b += lr * y[i]
                acc = np.mean(np.sign(X @ w + b) == y)
                if acc > best_acc:            # keep the best in the "pocket"
                    best_w, best_b, best_acc = w.copy(), b, acc
    return best_w, best_b, best_acc
_, _, acc = pocket(Xo, yo)
print(f"pocket algorithm best accuracy: {acc:.4f}")

# Logistic regression has no such problem -- it optimises a smooth loss:
print("logistic regression accuracy:",
      LogisticRegression().fit(Xo, yo).score(Xo, yo).round(4))

# =====================================================================
# 6. DEFECT 2 -- HARD OUTPUT, AND A ZERO GRADIENT
# =====================================================================
test = np.array([[4.2, 4.2],    # sitting almost ON the boundary
                 [8.0, 8.0]])   # far inside the positive region
print("\nperceptron output:", np.sign(test @ w + b))
# +1 and +1 -- IDENTICAL. No notion of confidence.

lr_model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, np.where(y > 0, 1, 0))
print("logistic probabilities:", lr_model.predict_proba(test)[:, 1].round(4))
# 0.53 and 0.9999 -- the second is far more confident. THIS is what you need
# to rank customers by risk or to move the decision threshold (Topic 53).

# The step function's derivative is zero everywhere it is defined:
def step(z):  return (z >= 0).astype(float)
eps = 1e-5
for z0 in [-3.0, -0.5, 0.5, 3.0]:
    d = (step(z0 + eps) - step(z0 - eps)) / (2 * eps)
    print(f"z={z0:+.1f}: d(step)/dz = {d:.1f}")
# 0.0 everywhere -- gradient descent has nothing to descend.
# The sigmoid fixes this (Topic 45): d(sigma)/dz = sigma*(1-sigma) > 0.

# =====================================================================
# 7. SKLEARN'S PERCEPTRON
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
p = Perceptron(eta0=0.1, max_iter=1000, tol=None, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nsklearn Perceptron: A={p.coef_[0][0]:.3f} B={p.coef_[0][1]:.3f} "
      f"C={p.intercept_[0]:.3f}  test acc {p.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print("it has no predict_proba:", not hasattr(p, "predict_proba"))
# Exactly defect 2, in the API itself.
Worked Examples
One perceptron update
Decision rule: predict $1$ if $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b \ge 0$. Start with $w = (1,1)$, $b = -3$, learning rate $\eta = 1$.
Step 1 – a positive point is wrong. Point $x = (1,1)$, label $y = 1$:
\text{score} = 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1 - 3 = -1 < 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat y = 0 \neq y
The point lies on the wrong side of the line.
Step 2 – perceptron trick. For a misclassified positive point, move the boundary toward it:
w \leftarrow w + \eta x = (1,1) + 1\cdot(1,1) = (2,2), \qquad b \leftarrow b + \eta = -2
Step 3 – recheck. New score $= 2 + 2 - 2 = 2 \ge 0$, so the point is now correctly classified.

Negative points. For a misclassified negative point (label $0$) the rule subtracts instead: $w \leftarrow w - \eta x$, $b \leftarrow b - \eta$. The same two cases in one line: $w \leftarrow w + \eta\,(y-\hat y)\,x$.

Why the trick is not used in practice. It converges only when the data are linearly separable, and it gives no probabilities. Logistic regression replaces the hard step with a sigmoid and updates with the gradient of log loss, which keeps the same update shape but works on non-separable data too.
Summary
Everything on one page

items: Data should be linearly separable.

We use the general equation of a line:
 $y=mx+b \to Ax+By+C=0$. The goal is to find $A$, $B$, $C$.

$A$ and $B$ decide the direction of the line; $C$ decides where
 the line sits. The vector $(A,B)$ is normal to the boundary and the
 sign of $Ax+By+C$ gives the class.

The general form is used because it handles vertical lines, generalises
 to $n$ dimensions, and makes the decision rule a single expression.

Adjust $A$, $B$, $C$ again and again until the line separates the
 data: on a misclassified point,
 $w\leftarrow w+\eta y_ix_i$ and $b\leftarrow b+\eta y_i$.

Each update provably improves the offending point's score by
 $\eta(\|x_i\|^2+1)$, rotating the boundary towards it.

The Perceptron Convergence Theorem guarantees at most $(R/\gamma)^2$
 mistakes if the data is separable — and no convergence at
 all if it is not.

Defect 1: it returns an arbitrary separating line. SVM fixes this
 with the maximum margin; logistic regression with maximum likelihood.

Defect 2: the output is hard $0$ or $1$, so there is no
 confidence and, because the step function is flat, no gradient to
 descend. This is why the sigmoid replaces it in Topic 45.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why use $Ax+By+C=0$ instead of $y=mx+c$?

Because $y=mx+c$ cannot represent a vertical line, does not generalise to more
than two dimensions, and does not directly give a decision rule. The general form
handles all three: $(A,B)$ is the normal vector, and the sign of the expression is
the class.
Q. What does the perceptron update actually do geometrically?

It adds a scaled copy of the misclassified point to the weight vector, rotating
the normal — and therefore the boundary — so that the offending point moves
towards the correct side. The score for that point changes by
$\eta(\|x_i\|^2+1)$ in the right direction.
Q. What happens if the data is not linearly separable?

The perceptron never terminates. It keeps finding mistakes and keeps updating, and
the boundary oscillates indefinitely. The pocket algorithm patches this by keeping
the best weights seen, but there is no principled objective being optimised.
Q. Why can't you train a perceptron with gradient descent?

Because the step activation is flat everywhere and discontinuous at zero, so its
derivative is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the boundary. There is no
slope to follow. The sigmoid replaces it precisely because it is smooth and has a
non-zero derivative $\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$.
Q. If the data is separable, isn't any separating line fine?

No. A line passing a hair from the nearest point has 100% training accuracy and
will generalise badly. The perceptron cannot distinguish it from a well-centred
line, because its only criterion is zero mistakes. SVM's maximum margin and
logistic regression's maximum likelihood are two different principled answers.
Q. How does the perceptron relate to logistic regression?

Same linear score $w^{\!\top}x+b$; different activation and different objective.
Replace the step with a sigmoid and you get probabilities; add the log-loss and
you get something differentiable that can be optimised by gradient descent and
that works on non-separable data. That is Topics 45 and 46.
